newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists leave asset sale options open.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists leave asset sale options open.

text.p: French Socialists, long opposed to selling off state-owned assets, may be forced by economic realities into a limited privatisation programme if they win a parliamentary majority in elections on Sunday, analysts said.

They believe that a government of the left will have to overcome its ideological objections and sell minority stakes in public companies to raise money for its ambitious job creation and work week reduction plans.

"There were fears the privatisation programme would be stopped, but there is a growing realisation a Socialist-led government will also have to sell shares. The amounts involved are enormous," said Olivier Blitz of brokers IFF.

Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin told Europe 1 radio on Tuesday that his party did not plan to privatise telecommunications operator France Telecom. The party has also said it would halt other privatisations planned by the ruling centre-right government.

That government, led by Prime Minister Alain Juppe, planned to sell 30 to 35 percent in the telecoms operator in what could be the country's biggest market operation with the company valued at some 160 to 210 billion francs ($28-37 billion).
The Socialists' economic plans aim to create 700,000 new jobs, with 350,000 in the public sector, and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay.

"Personally, I think a left-wing government would postpone the France Telecom sale but not cancel it, they need the money," said a head trader at a German bank, adding he expected the telecom sale in September.

Analysts said the Socialist Party is intentionally vague about the sale of state assets, waiting for the final outcome of the election to gauge the power of the Communist Party and weigh the concessions needed to get their support.

In the first round, the Socialists won 23.53 percent of the votes, Communists 9.94 percent and the ecologists 6.81 percent. The ruling RPR scored 15.7 percent and UDF 14.21 percent. The National Front took 14.94 percent.
If victorious, the Socialist Party aims to conduct an audit of France's public finances because it believes the state of the economy is worse than the centre-right government admits.
Official sources have said the deficit may be between 20 and 40 billion francs more than forecast, but Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said deficit reduction plans were on target.
Analysts say the outcome of the audit will allow the Socialists to persuade voters that partial sales of state companies are needed to balance the books.

Some Socialist officials, party spokesman Francois Hollande among them, say France Telecom will remain entirely in state hands. But others, such as Martine Aubry, a possible Socialist prime minister, say a partial sale is possible.

Hollande said on Monday a Socialist government would likely hold on to the 37.5 billion francs special pension transfer payment France Telecom made as part of a legal status change in the run-up to its sale.
Jospin, who had promised to consult the staff of France Telecom on its privatisation, has lately added new nuances to his statements on the issue.
On Tuesday, Jospin said such a consultation would only serve to inform the government which had the prerogative to decide.
"It's not the staff of France Telecom who decide on the privatisation of a very large company. That is a decision of the state, of the public powers," he told Europe 1 radio.
"Our position is not to privatise France Telecom," he added. "We could very well ask (staff) their opinion, it will be an element that enters into the decision, no more," he said.
Another pending privatisation is the sale of a 58-percent stake in defence electronics group Thomson-CSF.

Juppe's government planned to decide before the end of June whether to sell Thomson-CSF to engineering group Alcatel Alsthom and Dassault Industries or to conglomerate Lagardere Groupe and its European allies.
The Socialist Party said it would not complete this privatisation. ($ = 5.715 French Francs)
